---
title: "EOS Reimagined Manager"
description: "Development plan for the Windows and Linux game, instance, configuration, installation, and diagnostic manager."
---

## Objective

Build a novice-friendly desktop manager for Windows and Linux that turns the existing drop-in SDK,
configuration system, alpha runner, import census, and trace sink into one safe workflow:

1. find an installed game;
2. identify the EOS library it actually loads;
3. install or update the matching EOS Reimagined artifact without losing the original;
4. select a named local instance and edit every supported configuration field;
5. launch through the game's normal launcher;
6. collect, inspect, and bundle that run's diagnostics; and
7. restore the original SDK on demand.

The first acceptance target is Risk of Rain 2 over LAN between Windows and Linux/Proton. The manager
must generalize from that target rather than hard-code it. It is an operational front end for the
alpha, not a replacement for the behavioral work real-game traces will uncover.

## Place in the roadmap

The manager is the user-facing half of the operational-alpha milestone. Its minimum viable slice is
allowed to precede the first long in-game alpha because it removes installation and evidence-
collection mistakes, but a feature-complete launcher must not delay that alpha.

The planned [external social companion](companion-client.qmd) remains a separate control protocol and
SDK milestone. Its eventual GUI can live in this application's shell and reuse its game/instance
registry, but the manager must work without a running game and the companion must work without
permission to modify game files.

## Evidence behind the design

Two existing tools are useful boundaries, not code dependencies:

- [Deadlock Mod Manager](https://github.com/deadlock-mod-manager/deadlock-mod-manager) finds Steam
  with `steamlocate`, includes native and Flatpak Steam roots, allows manual path correction, and
  launches with `steam://run/<appid>//<arguments>`. It does **not** use a private Steam API to edit a
  game's saved launch options.
- [PartyDeck](https://github.com/partydeck/partydeck) creates real per-profile environments by
  launching executables itself through Gamescope, bubblewrap, UMU/Proton, separate prefixes, and
  directory overlays. That is powerful, Linux-specific orchestration with a much larger failure
  surface than this manager's ordinary one-instance-per-machine use case.

The resulting launch rule is important: a Steam URI can pass game arguments, but it cannot reliably
inject a new process environment into a Steam client that is already running. Editing Steam's private
`localconfig.vdf` while Steam is running is also unsupported and risks being overwritten. The basic
manager therefore uses normal Steam launch plus the bounded bootstrap descriptor below. Direct
launch and multi-instance orchestration are separate, capability-tested modes.

The GUI toolkit baseline is
[FLTK 1.4.5](https://github.com/fltk/fltk/releases/tag/release-1.4.5), pinned and
checksum-recorded. It is small, CMake-native,
supports Windows and Linux, can be statically packaged under its license exception, and builds in
C++11 mode. It must remain linked only into the manager executable; the replacement SDK library
gains no GUI dependency.

## Non-negotiable boundaries

- All project code remains strict C++11. The manager is not an exception.
- The SDK shared library stays headless and does not start, install, or depend on the manager.
- Portable manager behavior lives in a headless library. FLTK callbacks adapt UI state to that
  library; they do not perform file transactions or parse Steam data themselves.
- OS APIs remain under `src/platform/`, including the Windows registry, process enumeration, shell
  opening, module paths, and Linux desktop/Flatpak launch adapters.
- No undocumented Steam IPC, Steam credentials, Steam Web API key, or direct mutation of
  `localconfig.vdf` is required for the supported path.
- No game file is changed without an explicit action and a recoverable, hash-verified transaction.
- An unknown or externally changed file is never overwritten by Restore, Repair, or cleanup.
- The manager does not bypass anti-cheat, attest game ownership, contact Epic, or add Internet
  traversal. LAN remains the network boundary.
- The packaged application has no Python, Node, browser, or system-FLTK runtime requirement.

## Product model

The UI and state model must keep these concepts distinct:

| Object | Identity | Owns |
|---|---|---|
| Steam installation | platform + canonical root | library discovery method and launch adapter |
| Game installation | Steam app id + canonical install root, or a generated manual id | detected EOS targets and install state |
| EOS target | canonical SDK path + binary kind | original backup, staged artifact hash, transaction state |
| Managed instance | process-unique manager id and user slug | data directory, `profile.key`, `eosr.json`, trace runs |
| Diagnostic run | run id from `runtime.json` | trace files, stdout/launch metadata, census, bundle status |
| Configuration preset | manager id | reusable non-identity settings; applying it never copies a profile key |

A profile key is a player's identity, not a cosmetic preset. Copying a preset must not clone it.
Deleting an instance must warn that its profile identity will be lost and offer to export or retain
the key. Two machines must never be provisioned from the same instance directory.

## On-disk layout

The manager's root follows the platform convention:

- Windows: `%LOCALAPPDATA%\eos-reimagined-manager`
- Linux: `$XDG_DATA_HOME/eos-reimagined-manager`, falling back to
  `~/.local/share/eos-reimagined-manager`

The portable logical layout is:

```text
manager-root/
├── manager.json
├── logs/
├── artifacts/<release-id>/
│   ├── manifest.json
│   ├── EOSSDK-Win64-Shipping.dll
│   └── libEOSSDK-Linux-Shipping.so
└── games/<game-id>/
    ├── game.json
    └── instances/<instance-slug>/
        └── data/
            ├── eosr.json
            ├── profile.key
            └── traces/run-.../
                ├── runtime.json
                ├── trace.jsonl
                └── trace.N.jsonl
```

For native Steam and native Windows, the instance payload is physically under that logical
`instances/` path. Flatpak Steam cannot see the native host manager root: its persistent app data is
mounted as the user's home inside the sandbox. For Flatpak games, registry state, logs, target
records, and artifacts remain under the canonical manager root, while the one authoritative
instance payload is stored privately at this host path:

```text
~/.var/app/com.valvesoftware.Steam/.local/share/eos-reimagined-manager/
└── games/<game-id>/instances/<instance-slug>/data/
```

Inside the Flatpak runtime that payload appears at
`~/.local/share/eos-reimagined-manager/games/<game-id>/instances/<instance-slug>/data/`. It is not a
copy or mirror, so there remains exactly one `profile.key` per managed instance. Manager state stores
the actual host path and the target-runtime path separately.

Manager metadata uses process-unique ids; display names and slugs are not database keys. Paths in
metadata are absolute, UTF-8 at the portable boundary, and converted to/from UTF-16 only in the
Win32 platform implementation. Writes use a temporary sibling, flush, and replace. A manager-owned
file carries a schema version and is bounded before parsing.

Manager logs must contain operations and error codes, not profile-key bytes, credentials, raw EOS
ids, or packet payloads. Support bundles reuse the current sanitizer and never include
`profile.key`, original SDK backups, or manager registry state.

## Bootstrap descriptor: the Steam-safe configuration seam

### Why it is required

`EOSR_DATA_DIR` is deliberately not an `eosr.json` key because it locates that file. A GUI launched
through an already-running Steam client cannot portably inject it into the game process. Falling back
to the platform default would make every managed game share one config and would make a selected
instance mostly cosmetic.

### Contract to implement before the GUI

An optional `eosr-bootstrap.json` sits beside the replaced EOS library and contains only:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "data_dir": "an absolute manager-owned path in the target runtime's path syntax"
}
```

Resolution order for the data directory becomes:

1. non-empty `EOSR_DATA_DIR`;
2. a valid sibling bootstrap descriptor; then
3. the existing platform default.

`EOSR_CONFIG`, environment field overrides, and the contents of `eosr.json` keep their existing
precedence after the data directory is selected. The descriptor is not a second configuration file.

The descriptor is read once during `EOS_Initialize`, capped at 4 KiB, required to be a top-level
object with an exact supported version and an absolute, NUL-free path **as seen by that library**.
Duplicate keys or malformed JSON reject the whole descriptor. An invalid descriptor falls back safely
and becomes a structured configuration diagnostic once tracing/logging is available. A missing
descriptor preserves today's behavior byte-for-byte.

The manager stores both the host path and the target-runtime path. They are identical for
non-sandboxed native Linux and native Windows. For a Windows DLL under Proton, the descriptor needs
a Windows path such as
`Z:\\home\\...`, not a blindly copied POSIX path. The Linux platform adapter must inspect the selected
prefix's `dosdevices` mappings and prove that the translated path resolves back to the manager-owned
host directory. If no safe mapping exists, managed instance selection is disabled for that launch
adapter with a manual fallback; it never guesses. Persistent identities stay outside a disposable
Proton prefix by default.

Flatpak Steam adds a host-to-sandbox mapping before either native Linux or Proton path syntax is
chosen. The manager derives the app-data root only from a canonical discovered Flatpak Steam root,
requires the instance to remain under its private manager-owned subtree, and proves that the
sandbox-visible path maps back to that exact host directory. A Windows target then passes that
runtime path through the selected prefix's `dosdevices` mapping. A host path with the same visible
spelling but outside the Flatpak app-data root is an alias, not proof, and is refused.

The library locates its own module through a platform shim: the loaded DLL path on Windows (including
under Wine/Proton) and the loaded shared-object path on Linux. No current-working-directory lookup is
allowed.

The manager writes the descriptor as part of the installation transaction and records its hash.
Restore removes or restores it only when its current hash still matches manager state. It contains no
private key and points outside the game directory; profile material remains in the managed data
directory.

One game installation has one active bootstrap descriptor. This handles the normal case of one local
player per machine. Concurrent instances with different data directories need a real per-process
launcher or isolated game views and are explicitly deferred to the advanced launcher phase; changing
the descriptor between overlapping launches is forbidden.

## Steam and game discovery

### Steam roots

The discovery adapter checks, then allows the user to correct, these sources:

- Windows: `HKCU\Software\Valve\Steam` (`SteamPath`/`SteamExe`), standard install fallbacks, then
  every library in `steamapps\libraryfolders.vdf`.
- Native Linux: `~/.steam/steam`, `~/.steam/root`, and `~/.local/share/Steam`, then every VDF library.
- Flatpak Steam: `~/.var/app/com.valvesoftware.Steam/.local/share/Steam`,
  `~/.var/app/com.valvesoftware.Steam/data/Steam`, and compatible legacy roots, then every VDF
  library.

The VDF reader is bounded and supports old and current `libraryfolders.vdf` shapes, escaped strings,
Windows paths, arbitrary mounted libraries, malformed entries, and duplicate app references. An
`appmanifest_<appid>.acf` is evidence, but the resolved install directory and its files must exist.
Games are keyed by app id plus canonical install path so two libraries and moved installations are
not conflated.

A user can add a non-Steam or missed game by choosing its root. Manual entries go through the same
EOS scan and safety checks; they do not need a fabricated Steam app id.

### EOS target discovery

The manager searches boundedly for the canonical Windows and Linux SDK names and classifies the
actual file as PE or ELF rather than assuming the host OS. A Windows game under Proton therefore gets
the Windows DLL. Multiple candidates are presented; none is changed until the user selects or an
inspection report proves which one is used.

`inspect_game` becomes library behavior, not a required external Python process. Its report is stored
with the game and can still be exported in the existing `inspection.json` schema. The Python tool
remains available for automation and both implementations share conformance fixtures.

## Installation and restoration state machine

The manager recognizes these visible states:

- **Original** — a non-EOS-Reimagined SDK is present and no manager transaction owns it.
- **Installed (current)** — the file hash matches the selected bundled artifact and a verified
  original backup exists.
- **Installed (other build)** — it is recognizably EOS Reimagined but not the selected artifact.
- **Externally changed** — manager state exists but the live file no longer matches the staged hash.
- **Recovery required** — a transaction was interrupted and its journal/backup is intact.
- **Original unknown** — an EOS Reimagined file was installed outside the manager and no verified
  backup exists.
- **Missing**, **ambiguous**, or **unwritable** — no safe automatic action is available.

Install/Update performs the proven alpha-runner sequence with a versioned journal:

1. canonicalize and reject a symlinked target;
2. refuse while the game or target library is in use;
3. hash the live target and selected release artifact;
4. create an exclusive original backup and verify its hash;
5. write and flush the recovery journal;
6. replace through a temporary sibling;
7. verify the staged hash;
8. write/verify the bootstrap descriptor; and
9. record the completed state centrally without deleting recovery evidence.

Restore verifies the journal, current staged hash, and backup hash before replacing anything. If
Steam or another process changed the live file, the manager leaves both files untouched and offers
Open Location and Steam's Verify Installed Files workflow. No operation silently adopts an existing
backup, follows a target symlink, or overwrites an unrecognized `.original` file.

Repair means “re-stage the selected known artifact after all ownership checks”; it never means
“discard whatever is there.” Uninstall means restore the verified original and remove only
manager-owned sidecars whose hashes match. A Steam update replacing the SDK becomes Externally
changed, not an excuse to restore stale bytes over the update.

## Launch modes

### Standard Steam launch — required for the first release

The manager selects the active instance, commits its `eosr.json`, commits the bootstrap descriptor,
then launches the app with Steam's URI/command mechanism. Windows uses the discovered Steam
executable or registered URI handler. Linux chooses the detected native or Flatpak adapter and has a
portal/`xdg-open` fallback. No environment injection is claimed in this mode.

The manager records a launch attempt and watches the selected instance's trace directory for a new
`runtime.json`. Seeing it changes the UI to Running and proves the replacement loaded. Failure to see
it within a bounded interval becomes an actionable warning, not a permanent spinner. The user can
still mark the launch as finished and open the game/log directories.

### Direct/custom launch — optional per-game capability

A manual executable and argument list may be configured for non-Steam titles or titles proven to
work when started directly. Arguments are stored as an array, never concatenated into a shell
command. The child receives `EOSR_DATA_DIR`, `EOSR_RUN_DIR`, and other selected overrides directly.
This mode must not be auto-selected merely because an executable was found.

### Advanced multi-instance launch — later milestone

PartyDeck-style direct Proton/UMU launching, separate prefixes, overlay game directories, and several
simultaneous local identities are handler-driven capabilities, not generic assumptions. They require
their own acceptance matrix and disk-space/error UI. The first manager release can create and switch
named instances but launches only one active instance for a given game installation at a time.

The manager never edits Steam's saved launch-options VDF. A Copy Launch Recipe action may generate
documented user instructions as a fallback, but it must label them as manual and reversible.

## Configuration experience

The form is generated from one shared field description table so the GUI, defaults, validation,
writer, and tests cannot drift. It exposes every field in the
[configuration contract](../../users/configuration.qmd):

- Identity: display name and instance label.
- Language: locale.
- Network: enable/disable, discovery-port first/last, and bounded IPv4 peer seeds, with a reminder
  that every participant must share the port range and seed list.
- Diagnostics: trace level, trace directory, file cap, rotation count, and ordinary EOS log level.
- Compatibility: `enable_overlay` and `unlock_dlcs`, visibly marked unavailable rather than shown as
  working toggles.
- Advanced: active instance data/config locations, with Open Location rather than editable identity
  paths in the basic view.

The editor validates before Save using the exact SDK rules and shows truncation/clamping before it
happens. Save is atomic. A user-owned existing `eosr.json` is imported with a backup; unknown valid
keys are preserved, and a malformed file is never overwritten without explicit Replace confirmation.
Reset affects the form, not the profile key.

Environment variables still outrank the GUI file. After a run, the manager reads `runtime.json` and
shows configured versus effective values and each effective source (`environment`, `file`, or
`default`). Older runtime files without provenance remain readable and are labeled source
unavailable. Before a run it warns that inherited `EOSR_*` variables may override the form but does
not modify the user's global environment.

The GUI labels the four name roles explicitly: manager label, EOS Reimagined `display_name`, the
effective runtime name, and the game/Steam-owned nickname. Renaming the manager label is cosmetic and
does not rewrite `eosr.json`; the game nickname is never claimed to be synchronized. `runtime.json`
is authoritative for the name EOS Reimagined actually announced, while `profile.key` alone determines
the persistent identity.

## User interface

The first release has four primary views:

1. **Games** — discovered/manual games, install health, EOS targets, artifact version, and actions:
   Configure, Install/Update, Repair, Restore, Launch, Open Game Folder.
2. **Instances** — create, select, rename, export identity backup, open data folder, and delete with
   identity-loss confirmation.
3. **Runs** — active/completed/incomplete runs with build, OS/Wine, trace level, timestamps, key
   lifecycle milestones, Open Folder, Build Support Bundle, and Delete.
4. **Settings/Health** — Steam installations and libraries, artifact verification, manager log,
   release identity, and a copyable system report.

The first-run wizard performs discovery, asks the user to choose a game, explains the original-file
backup, creates one instance with a display name, defaults tracing to `lifecycle` for alpha builds,
and stops at a final review before modifying the game.

Errors name the object and next action: “Steam library is read-only — open folder,” “game is still
running — close it before Restore,” “Steam replaced this DLL — verify files or inspect manually,” not
raw errno/Win32 text alone. Technical details remain expandable and copyable.

Open Location uses `explorer.exe /select,`/Shell APIs on Windows and the desktop opener or portal on
Linux. The platform layer reports failure; it never assumes a spawned opener succeeded.

## Diagnostic runs and bundles

The manager indexes run directories from `runtime.json`, tolerates a torn final JSONL line, and does
not load an unbounded trace into memory. Summaries are streamed and cached by file size/mtime/hash.
At minimum a run summary shows:

- whether the SDK initialized and which exact build loaded;
- discovery listen port;
- discover, handshake, adopt, and drop counts/reasons;
- Sessions/Lobby search and join outcomes;
- P2P open/close and byte counts; and
- stubbed EOS functions invoked by the game.

Bundle creation uses the existing deny-by-default sanitizer and writes a new sibling directory or
archive. It reports exactly which files were included or excluded. The GUI never labels an unsanitized
run directory “shareable.” User-selected instance labels are identity-bearing metadata just like
display names: the bundle rewrites the runtime label and every trace-record `inst` field to the stable
bundle-local pseudonym `instance#0`. The `config.sources.instance_label` provenance remains intact
because it describes where the value came from, not the value itself.

## Architecture and source layout

Planned targets:

```text
eosr_manager_core       # portable C++11 domain logic; no GUI or OS headers
eosr_manager            # FLTK executable; thin presentation/adaptation layer
manager_tests           # core, fixture, and state-machine tests
manager_platform_tests  # native platform integration tests
```

Planned source ownership:

```text
src/manager/            # models, services, parsers, transactions, run index
src/manager/ui/         # FLTK widgets and view models only
src/platform/           # Windows/Linux Steam, process, shell, registry, module-path adapters
tests/manager/           # portable fixtures and platform integration tests
third_party/fltk/       # one pinned, checksum-recorded upstream release
```

The manager core returns typed results with stable error codes and optional details. It does not
throw errors across the UI boundary. Long scans and hashes run on bounded worker jobs; the FLTK event
thread only applies completed snapshots. Cancellation leaves transactions untouched once mutation
has begun; critical transactions run to a recoverable terminal state.

`BUILD_MANAGER` is a CMake option. Normal SDK targets do not link FLTK. CI and release packaging
enable it explicitly. A small headless `eosr-manager-cli` may expose scan/status/install/restore/
bundle through the same core for automation and fault-injection tests; it is not a second
implementation.

## Test strategy

### Portable unit tests

- VDF: old/new library formats, escapes, Unicode, Windows drive/UNC strings, duplicate libraries,
  missing braces, oversized tokens/files, and hostile nesting.
- Game discovery: native Linux, Windows, Proton, multiple libraries, duplicate app ids, stale
  manifests, missing install roots, manual games, multiple EOS candidates, PE/ELF classification.
- Configuration: every field/default/alias, validation boundary, unknown-key preservation,
  malformed-file refusal, atomic-write recovery, environment precedence, and GUI schema parity with
  `resolve_config`.
- Instances: slug collisions, rename, stable ids, profile separation, preset copying without key
  copying, active-instance switching, deletion safeguards.
- Install state: every visible state and transition, current/old/unknown artifacts, missing or
  changed backup, existing sidecars, symlinks, interrupted operations, and idempotent recovery.
- Runs: live/incomplete/rotated/torn traces, bounded streaming, summary extraction, cache
  invalidation, display-name and instance-label sanitization, private-file exclusion, and exactly one
  JSONL delimiter after each rewritten support-trace record.
- Launch requests: argument arrays, quoting edge cases, spaces/Unicode, native/Flatpak Steam adapter
  selection, timeouts, and no shell interpolation.

### Fault-injection tests

Every mutating file step is injectable and tested with failure before and after it: create, write,
flush, close, rename, hash, permission change, and cleanup. Restarting from each persisted journal
must either finish safely or explain why user action is required. Disk-full, read-only library,
locked DLL, antivirus quarantine, and external modification are explicit cases.

### Platform integration

- Native Windows/MSVC: registry discovery, UTF-16/non-ASCII/long paths, alternate drives, UNC paths,
  file sharing violations, process detection, Explorer actions, and Steam URI construction.
- Linux: XDG paths, native and Flatpak Steam layouts, arbitrary mounted libraries, permissions,
  symlinks, `xdg-open`/portal failure, and case-sensitive SDK names.
- Proton/Wine: the Windows DLL and sibling bootstrap descriptor are read through Win32 inside Wine;
  host-to-Windows path translation is verified against `dosdevices`, including a missing/changed
  `Z:` mapping; Flatpak Steam fixtures additionally prove the host-to-sandbox namespace hop and
  reject the unrelated host-home alias; and a Linux manager correctly classifies/stages that DLL.
- Fake Steam roots are temporary fixtures; tests never modify a developer's real Steam metadata.

### ABI and end-to-end

- A real loaded `.so` and `.dll` resolve the bootstrap descriptor and emit the selected instance path
  in `runtime.json`; missing/invalid descriptors preserve fallback behavior.
- The manager installs into a fake game, launches the existing ABI probe, observes its run, bundles
  it, restores the original, and proves every final hash.
- Two managed probe instances with distinct data directories mesh and retain distinct profiles.
- Opt-in manual acceptance covers Windows Steam, native Linux Steam, Flatpak Steam + Proton, and the
  real Risk of Rain 2 install. These tests are never run against a real library automatically.

### GUI and packaging

- View-model tests cover enabled/disabled actions and exact error-to-action mapping.
- A headless smoke test creates every primary view and processes one event loop iteration.
- Windows and Linux packaged binaries start on clean runners without Python or an installed FLTK.
- Package verification checks executable/artifact hashes, licenses, manifest membership, build id,
  and that the Linux package contains both SDK artifacts for native games and Proton.

## CI and release gates

Add manager jobs without weakening the existing alpha release gates:

- Linux release build and manager-core/platform tests.
- Native MSVC x64 release build and manager-core/platform tests.
- MinGW/Wine build for the SDK and bootstrap ABI tests.
- Linux ASan + UBSan for all headless manager code and fault-injection tests.
- GUI build/smoke and deterministic package verification on Windows and Linux.

The release workflow remains manually dispatched. A manager release candidate is produced only
after the SDK artifacts it embeds pass their current Linux, Wine, MSVC, sanitizer, ABI, export, and
package gates. The manager and embedded artifacts share one release manifest and exact source
revision.

Initial packages:

- Windows x64 ZIP (and later an installer) containing `EOSReimaginedManager.exe`, the Windows SDK
  artifact, manifest, licenses, and user guide.
- Linux x86_64 tar archive plus an AppImage candidate containing the manager and both SDK artifacts.
  The tar archive remains the fallback when FUSE/AppImage integration is unavailable.

The manager itself is initially a native host application, not a Flatpak. A sandboxed manager cannot
reliably mutate arbitrary Steam libraries without a portal/permission design; Flatpak packaging is a
later distribution milestone, while Flatpak **Steam discovery** is required from the first release.

## Delivery phases and acceptance gates

### Phase 0 — contracts and packaging spike

- Record an ADR for the bootstrap descriptor and precedence.
- Pin/build FLTK under strict C++11 on Linux and MSVC without touching the SDK link surface.
- Prototype normal Steam URI launch for native Windows, native Linux, and Flatpak Steam.
- Confirm the bootstrap descriptor from native Linux, Windows, and the Windows DLL under Wine.

Gate: a tiny packaged manager window starts on both hosts, and loaded-library tests prove the selected
data directory without any Steam VDF mutation.

### Phase 1 — headless manager core

- Models and versioned manager state.
- Steam/VDF and manual-game discovery.
- EOS target inspection and release-artifact verification.
- Install/update/restore transaction and recovery CLI.
- Instance/config creation and atomic writes.
- Run index and bundle service.

Gate: all workflows run headlessly against fixtures and the ABI probe, with red-before-green failure
tests at every transaction boundary.

### Phase 2 — first usable GUI

- First-run wizard, Games, Instances, Runs, and Health views.
- Install/Update/Restore, full configuration form, standard Steam launch, run detection, Open
  Location, and sanitized bundle creation.
- Risk of Rain 2 recognition without a game-specific install script.

Gate: a Windows novice and a Linux/Flatpak-Steam novice can each install, choose a name, enable
`lifecycle` tracing, launch through Steam, find the new run, make a support bundle, and restore the
original SDK without a terminal.

This gate is sufficient to resume the real two-machine LAN alpha. Later manager features do not block
behavioral fixes found by that test.

### Phase 3 — alpha operations and hardening

- Run summaries and cross-machine fingerprint comparison.
- Artifact update/repair UX and Steam-update detection.
- Crash recovery on application start.
- Installer/AppImage polish, accessibility pass, localization-ready strings, and signed-build plan.
- Several-game generalization using census/run evidence.

Gate: interrupted installs recover deterministically, support bundles stay sanitized, and three
different EOS games complete the manager workflow even if their gameplay support differs.

### Phase 4 — advanced launch handlers

- Capability-tested direct launch profiles.
- Optional UMU/Proton handlers, separate prefixes, and isolated concurrent instances on Linux.
- A Windows multi-instance design only after a non-invasive launch method is proven.
- Import/export handler files with explicit compatibility metadata.

Gate: two concurrent local instances use distinct manager data directories without racing the shared
bootstrap descriptor or modifying Steam's saved launch options.

### Phase 5 — social companion in the same shell

- Implement the control-plane stages in the companion design.
- Add a Party view that discovers running SDK instances and lists authenticated join candidates.
- Keep manager file permissions separate from the loopback companion capability.

Gate: the same application can configure a game while it is stopped and deliver a documented
join-accepted event while it is running, with neither mode required for the other.

## First implementation sequence

The next development goal should take these in order and stop at a clean gate rather than opening all
phases at once:

1. bootstrap-descriptor ADR, implementation, and native/Wine loaded-library regression tests;
2. FLTK C++11 packaging spike and `eosr_manager_core`/UI target separation;
3. bounded VDF parser and Steam-root/library discovery fixtures;
4. manager state, game/EOS-target classification, and artifact manifest verification;
5. hash-verified install/restore state machine ported from the alpha runner with fault injection;
6. managed instance layout and shared configuration-field schema;
7. minimal Games/Configure/Install/Restore GUI;
8. standard Steam launch, run detection, Runs view, and support bundle action; then
9. the real Windows ↔ Linux/Proton Risk of Rain 2 alpha.

## Explicitly deferred

- Internet discovery, NAT traversal, and relay services.
- Anti-cheat support or bypass.
- Editing Steam's private per-user launch-options database.
- Automatic elevation or writing protected libraries as administrator/root.
- Downloading arbitrary SDK builds or self-updating before signed/checksummed update policy exists.
- Cloud synchronization of profile keys.
- Generic simultaneous multi-instance support in the first release.
- Rendering an in-game overlay; join actions belong to the external companion.

## Completion definition for the manager alpha

The manager alpha is complete when, on both Windows and Linux:

- Steam libraries (including Flatpak Steam on Linux) and a manual game can be discovered;
- the actual EOS target and required DLL/SO are correctly classified;
- install, update, interrupted recovery, and restore are hash-safe;
- every current EOS Reimagined configuration directive is editable or honestly marked unsupported;
- a named managed instance gets a stable isolated profile/config/trace directory;
- a normal Steam launch proves the selected SDK and instance through `runtime.json`;
- diagnostic runs can be opened and sanitized without a terminal;
- the package runs without development runtimes; and
- the Risk of Rain 2 Windows ↔ Linux/Proton LAN trial produces complete evidence for the next
  behavioral iteration.

## Integration status and remaining acceptance evidence

As of 2026-07-27, the Phase 0 through Phase 2 implementation is present in the integration branch.
The Linux, MinGW/Wine, sanitizer, deterministic-package, packaged-binary smoke, and Quarto gates pass
locally. The Flatpak-Steam Risk of Rain 2 workflow has also proved discovery, a hash-verified
installation, normal Steam launch, and that Proton loaded the exact managed Windows DLL.

The following acceptance evidence remains required before the manager alpha can be declared complete:

1. Run the native Windows/MSVC CI gate on the pushed revision and retain its artifacts. This gate is
   configured but was not executed on the Linux development host.
2. Complete the packaged GUI novice workflow on a native Windows machine: discover, install,
   configure a named instance, launch, inspect a run, create a sanitized support bundle, and restore.
3. Complete the equivalent packaged GUI novice workflow for Linux with Flatpak Steam, including the
   final restore step.
4. Capture a post-fix Risk of Rain 2 private-lobby diagnostic run and verify Connect copy success,
   bounded mapping/update calls, and no null-key avatar lookup failures.
5. Run the real Windows-to-Linux/Proton LAN alpha with the Windows peer, preserve sanitized evidence,
   and add red-before-green regressions for every behavioral failure it exposes.
6. Restore the original game DLL after the LAN alpha and verify the final hash. The current managed
   replacement must not be mistaken for completion of the restore gate.

Phase 3 and later work remains intentionally deferred until this evidence closes the Phase 2 gate.
